listening.title: Joining a weekend swimming course
listening.intro: You will hear a man phoning a sports centre about a swimming course.
listening.instructions: Complete the form. Write ONE WORD AND/OR A NUMBER for each answer.
lines: RECEPTIONIST: Good morning, Riverside Sports Centre. How can I help?
CALLER: Hello. I'd like to book a place on the adult swimming course for beginners.
RECEPTIONIST: Of course. Can I take your name, please?
CALLER: Yes, it's Daniel Hartley. That's H-A-R-T-L-E-Y.
RECEPTIONIST: Thank you. The beginners' course runs on Saturday mornings. Sorry, I'm looking at last year's timetable. This year it's on Sunday mornings.
CALLER: Sunday is fine. What time does it start?
RECEPTIONIST: The lesson starts at half past nine and finishes at half past ten.
CALLER: And how many weeks is the course?
RECEPTIONIST: It used to be eight weeks, but it's ten weeks now, so you get two extra lessons.
CALLER: Great. How much does it cost?
RECEPTIONIST: The full price is ninety-five pounds, but members pay seventy. Are you a member?
CALLER: No, I'm not, so I'll pay the full price.
RECEPTIONIST: All right. Is there anything you need to bring? Well, a towel, obviously, but the important thing is a padlock for the lockers. We don't provide those.
CALLER: I'll remember that. Where should I go when I arrive?
RECEPTIONIST: Please wait by the café on the ground floor. The instructor will meet the group there.

listening.title: How the recycling centre works
listening.intro: You will hear a guide explaining how a town recycling centre processes waste.
listening.instructions: Complete the flow chart. Write ONE WORD for each answer.
lines: GUIDE: Welcome, everyone, to the Northfield Recycling Centre. I'm going to explain what happens to your recycling from the moment it arrives.
GUIDE: First, the lorries drive onto a large scale, where the whole load is weighed. This tells us how much each area of the town is recycling.
GUIDE: Next, the load is tipped onto the floor of the main hall, and staff remove anything that obviously doesn't belong, such as garden hoses or old clothes, because these can damage the machines.
GUIDE: After that, everything goes onto a moving belt. Along the belt, powerful magnets lift out steel cans. Aluminium cans aren't magnetic, so they're separated later by a different machine.
GUIDE: Then the paper and card are blown upwards by jets of air, because they're lighter than glass and plastic. They're collected at the top of the machine.
GUIDE: The plastic bottles are sorted by a camera, which recognises different types of plastic by their colour and shape.

GUIDE: Finally, each material is pressed into large blocks called bales, which are stored outside until a buyer collects them. Some of you have asked whether glass is pressed too. It isn't: glass is crushed and kept in separate containers.
GUIDE: Right, let's go up to the viewing gallery so you can see the belt in action.

questions.q: Step 1: Each load is _____ on a large scale.
questions.evidence: the lorries drive onto a large scale, where the whole load is weighed

questions.q: Step 2: Staff remove items such as hoses and old _____.
questions.evidence: such as garden hoses or old clothes

questions.q: Step 3: _____ lift out steel cans from the belt.
questions.evidence: powerful magnets lift out steel cans

questions.q: Step 4: Paper and card are blown upwards by jets of _____.
questions.evidence: the paper and card are blown upwards by jets of air

questions.q: Step 5: A _____ sorts plastic bottles by colour and shape.
questions.evidence: The plastic bottles are sorted by a camera

questions.q: What happens to the glass?
options: It is crushed and kept separately
It is sent back to the shops
questions.key: It is crushed and kept separately
questions.evidence: It isn't: glass is crushed and kept in separate containers.

listening.title: Welcome talk at a summer festival
listening.intro: You will hear an organiser speaking to volunteers before a summer festival.
listening.instructions: Choose the correct letter, A, B, C or D.
lines: ORGANISER: Good morning, and thank you all for giving up your weekend to help at the Lakeside Festival. Before we start, I want to make sure everyone knows what to expect.

ORGANISER: Last year, our biggest problem wasn't the weather or the music. It was the queues at the main gate. So this year, we've opened a second entrance on Mill Road, and most of you will be working there in the morning.
ORGANISER: You'll each get a radio. Please don't use it for chatting; keep it for anything urgent, like a lost child or someone who feels unwell.

ORGANISER: A few of you asked about food. You won't need to bring a packed lunch, because every volunteer gets a free meal token for the food tents. You will need to bring water, though, as it's going to be hot.

ORGANISER: Now, I'm sometimes asked why we need so many volunteers when we could just hire security staff. The honest answer is that visitors tell us the friendly welcome is what makes this festival different, and that comes from you.
ORGANISER: Finally, if you're not sure about anything during the day, don't guess. Come and find one of the team leaders in the yellow jackets.

questions.evidence: It was the queues at the main gate.

listening.title: Planning a group presentation
listening.intro: You will hear two students, Amira and Leo, discussing a presentation about city transport.
listening.instructions: Choose the correct letter, A, B, C or D.
lines: AMIRA: So, Leo, we need to decide how to start our presentation on city transport. I thought we could open with some statistics about traffic.
LEO: Hmm, I'm not sure. Everyone else will probably start with numbers. What if we began with a short story about one person's journey to work? It might hold people's attention better.
AMIRA: That's a good point, actually. Statistics can come straight after that.
LEO: Agreed. Now, about the bike-sharing scheme. I read that it was very popular in the first year, but I think the newer figures are more useful.
AMIRA: Definitely. The early figures make it look like a huge success, but use dropped a lot when the price went up. We should be honest about that.
LEO: What about the tram extension? I was going to say it was a complete failure.
AMIRA: I wouldn't go that far. It was late and over budget, but passenger numbers are now higher than the planners predicted.
LEO: OK, so it's mixed, really. I'll present it that way.
AMIRA: For the final part, our tutor said she wants a recommendation, not just a summary.
LEO: Then let's recommend cheaper bike-sharing for students. That links our two main sections.
AMIRA: Perfect. I'll make the slides tonight, and you can write the story for the opening.

options: Statistics are too difficult to find
It may keep the audience interested
The tutor asked for a story

questions.evidence: It might hold people's attention better.

questions.evidence: use dropped a lot when the price went up. We should be honest about that.

options: It had problems but now has more passengers than expected

listening.title: Lecture: how honeybees find food
listening.intro: You will hear part of a biology lecture about how honeybees share information.
listening.instructions: Complete the notes. Write ONE WORD for each answer.
lines: LECTURER: Today I want to look at one of the most remarkable forms of communication in the animal world: the way honeybees tell each other where to find food.

LECTURER: When a worker bee discovers a good source of nectar, she returns to the hive and performs what scientists call a waggle dance. The dance takes place on the vertical surface of the honeycomb, inside the dark hive, so other bees follow it mainly by touch rather than by sight.

LECTURER: The direction of the dance tells the other bees the direction of the food. Straight up the honeycomb represents the direction of the sun. So if the bee dances at an angle of forty degrees to the right of vertical, the food is forty degrees to the right of the sun.
LECTURER: Distance is shown in a different way. It's the length of the waggle run, not the speed of the dance, that tells the bees how far to fly. A longer run means the food is further away.
LECTURER: Bees also need to judge quality. A bee that has found a particularly rich source repeats her dance many more times, which recruits more followers.

LECTURER: Interestingly, researchers have found that bees don't follow every dance. Younger foragers, in particular, often ignore dances and search on their own, which helps the colony discover new sources.
LECTURER: In the next session, we'll look at how changes in farming have affected these foraging patterns.

questions.q: Inside the hive, bees follow the dance mainly by _____.
questions.evidence: other bees follow it mainly by touch rather than by sight

questions.q: Straight up the honeycomb represents the direction of the _____.
questions.evidence: Straight up the honeycomb represents the direction of the sun.

questions.q: Distance is shown by the _____ of the waggle run.
questions.evidence: It's the length of the waggle run, not the speed of the dance

questions.q: A rich food source makes the bee _____ her dance many more times.
questions.evidence: A bee that has found a particularly rich source repeats her dance many more times

questions.q: _____ foragers often ignore dances and search alone.
questions.evidence: Younger foragers, in particular, often ignore dances and search on their own

questions.q: What will the next session be about?
options: The effect of farming changes on foraging
How young bees learn to dance
questions.key: The effect of farming changes on foraging
questions.evidence: we'll look at how changes in farming have affected these foraging patterns

listening.title: Reporting lost property
listening.intro: You will hear a woman calling a railway lost property office.
listening.instructions: Complete the notes. Write ONE WORD AND/OR A NUMBER for each answer.
lines: CLERK: Lost property office, good afternoon.
CALLER: Hi. I think I left my bag on a train yesterday.
CLERK: I'm sorry to hear that. What kind of bag is it?
CALLER: It's a small black backpack. Oh, sorry, it's dark blue, actually. It just looks black.
CLERK: Dark blue. And which train were you on?
CALLER: The one from Westbridge to the city. It left Westbridge at seven fifteen in the morning.
CLERK: OK, the seven fifteen. Do you remember which carriage you were in?
CALLER: I think it was carriage six. No, wait, I moved to carriage four because six was full.
CLERK: Carriage four. What was inside the bag?
CALLER: My laptop, a notebook and a water bottle. The laptop has a sticker of a mountain on it.
CLERK: That's helpful. Can I have a phone number in case we find it?
CALLER: Yes, it's oh-seven-seven, four-five-two, nine-three-eight-one.
CLERK: Thank you. We'll keep any found items for twenty-eight days, so do call back if you don't hear from us.
